notes: Human split-belt adaptation occurs within 10-20 stride cycles through reorganization of the stride cycle (support shortens and swing lengthens on the fast leg), with ipsilateral gastrocnemius activity scaling almost linearly with belt speed under proprioceptive control while the contralateral tibialis anterior is centrally modulated, revealing an ipsilateral-proprioceptive / contralateral-central coupling between the support phase of one leg and the swing phase of the other.
animal_study: The spinal contribution to split-belt adaptation could be isolated in decerebrate or spinal cats on a split-belt treadmill, testing whether ipsilateral extensor proprioceptive modulation and the contralateral flexor coupling persist without supraspinal control.
robot_sim: Implement split-belt adaptation in a biped model as ipsilateral proprioceptive extensor feedback that scales stance muscle activity with belt speed, plus a central contralateral coupling from support to opposite-limb swing; ablating the proprioceptive branch should abolish automatic speed matching.
flags: Abstract attributes the adaptation to 'proprioceptive feedback' without specifying afferent types or a specific pathway, so afferents and feedback were left empty.

notes: Shows that the synchronized state of nonlocally coupled Hodgkin-Huxley neurons with excitatory and inhibitory synaptic coupling is linearly unstable, and that its destabilization yields chimera states, wavy states, clustering, and spatiotemporal chaos, providing a mechanism by which spatially structured, partially synchronized activity can emerge in distributed oscillator networks without parameter heterogeneity.
robot_sim: Build a nonlocally coupled oscillator network with mixed excitatory/inhibitory coupling and test the stability of the synchronized state; parameter sweeps should reproduce chimera, clustering, wavy, and chaotic regimes, a caution for multi-limb CPG designs that assume synchrony.
flags: Pure nonlinear-dynamics paper (chimera states); no animal or afferent content. Likely included as oscillator-coordination background; scope decision for Ben.

notes: During fictive locomotion in high spinal paralyzed cats, forelimb nerve stimulation evokes EPSPs in hindlimb extensor motoneurons only during extension and in flexor motoneurons only during flexion, establishing that transmission in the descending excitatory propriospinal reflex pathway is cyclically gated at the lumbar level by the locomotor rhythm.
animal_study: Test the lumbar phase-gating by stimulating forelimb nerves at defined cycle phases while recording lumbar interneurons and motoneurons in reduced preparations, or section the descending propriospinal pathways to assess loss of forelimb-hindlimb coordination during overground locomotion.
robot_sim: Add forelimb-to-hindlimb excitatory propriospinal coupling to a quadruped CPG, gated by lumbar phase (excitation reaching extensor motoneurons during extension and flexor motoneurons during flexion); removing the phase gate should scramble interlimb coordination.
flags: Phase-gated descending propriospinal excitation from forelimb afferents to lumbar motoneurons fits no current Feedback vocabulary entry; consider 'propriospinal interlimb excitation, phase-gated'. Afferent types not specified in the abstract.

notes: Proposed that stable and flexible locomotion emerges as a global limit cycle produced by global entrainment between coupled neural oscillators, the musculoskeletal system, and the environment, rather than by tracking explicit trajectories; the simulated biped withstood mechanical perturbations and environmental changes, and switched between walking and running (with hysteresis) by changing a single nonspecific parameter.
animal_study: The global-entrainment principle could be tested in reduced animal preparations by imposing periodic mechanical perturbations during treadmill or fictive locomotion and quantifying phase locking of the neural rhythm to the mechanical load, as mutual neural-mechanical entrainment predicts.
robot_sim: Implement coupled neural oscillators with mutual inhibition, entrained with a musculoskeletal biped through sensorimotor feedback loops; verify perturbation resistance, environmental adaptation, and walk-run transitions with hysteresis under a single-parameter drive change, replicating the paper's claims.

notes: Imposed ramp movements of the hip during fictive locomotion in acute spinal curarized cats reset the locomotor rhythm with a phase-dependent sign, prolonging the cycle when applied early (during flexor activity) and markedly shortening it later, with direction-sensitive positive feedback on flexor bursts at the end of flexion and stronger flexor responses at more extended hip positions, demonstrating potent phase-specific peripheral control of the central pattern generator.
animal_study: Identify which hip receptor class carries the phase-reset signal by recording hip afferents during imposed ramp movements, or selectively denervate hip afferents and quantify the loss of phase-dependent cycle modulation during locomotion.
robot_sim: Implement a phase-dependent hip-angle reset input to the rhythm generator: early-cycle ramps prolong and late-cycle ramps shorten the cycle, with end-of-flexion directional sensitivity and position-dependent gain; ablating this input should remove the cycle-timing modulation.
flags: Hip-ramp phase reset and swing-triggering effects fit no current vocabulary entry; consider 'hip position afferent stance to swing'. The abstract does not specify the afferent type mediating the effect.

notes: Synthesizes cat walking evidence that feedback from muscle proprioceptors establishes the timing of major phase transitions, contributes to burst production, generates some features of the motor pattern, and is required for adaptive modification after alterations in leg mechanics; argues that afferent signals likely reorganize the functioning of central networks, making 'afferent modulation of a hard-wired CPG' too simplistic a framework.
animal_study: The proposed reorganization of central network functioning by phasic afferent signals could be tested by recording identified central neurons during real stepping versus deafferented fictive locomotion, the comparison the abstract identifies as the missing experiment.
robot_sim: Model phase-transition timing and burst production as afferent-controlled processes rather than fixed CPG timing; ablate individual proprioceptive channels and quantify the loss of adaptive motor-pattern modification to altered leg mechanics.

notes: Implemented Brown's half-center CPG concept as reciprocally organized integrators whose parameters were optimized to satisfy the biomechanical requirements of overground locomotion, finding that the control signal driving each limb's CPG corresponds to the desired speed of forward progression; supports a scheme in which descending and sensory feedback inputs combine into a high-level command that sets forward velocity, with steering generated by differential speed commands to different limbs.
animal_study: Record spinal network activity across locomotor speeds in reduced preparations to test whether the combined descending-sensory drive corresponds to desired forward speed, and during turning to test for differential speed-command input across limbs.
robot_sim: Drive each limb's half-center CPG with a speed-command signal and implement steering as differential speed commands across limbs, with phase-duration characteristics matched by optimization; removing the sensory component of the combined drive should degrade velocity regulation.

notes: Intra-axonal recordings during fictive locomotion in decorticated cats show that all cutaneous primary afferents develop locomotor-rhythmic membrane potential fluctuations with two depolarization waves per cycle (maximal during flexor activity in the majority of units), demonstrating that the CPG phasically controls the efficacy of transmission in cutaneous pathways at a presynaptic level as part of the locomotor program.
animal_study: Test whether the phase of maximal cutaneous primary afferent depolarization shifts with locomotor speed or between motor tasks, or pharmacologically block the PAD mechanism to demonstrate the predicted task- and phase-dependent changes in cutaneous reflex transmission.
robot_sim: Implement phase-dependent presynaptic gating of cutaneous feedback channels: scale cutaneous synaptic gains by a locomotor-phase gate with maximal presynaptic inhibition phased to flexor activity, and compare reflex behavior against an ungated model.
flags: CPG-driven presynaptic (PAD) control of cutaneous afferents fits no current vocabulary entry; consider 'Cutaneous presynaptic inhibition'.

notes: Traces the spinal CPG concept from cats with complete spinal cord transection that recover locomotor function to evidence for a human spinal locomotor CPG drawn from treadmill-training recovery in incomplete spinal cord injury, framing locomotor rehabilitation as exploitation of spinal rhythm-generating circuitry conserved from cats to humans.
animal_study: The framework could seed longitudinal animal studies combining complete spinal transection with intense treadmill training and pharmacological neuromodulation to define the training parameters that drive recovery of spinal locomotor function.
robot_sim: Implement a spinal CPG block whose basic rhythmic activation survives removal of step-specific sensory feedback, mirroring transection-cat recovery, and study training-like adaptation regimes of the circuit in simulation.

notes: Argues from spinal-cord-stimulation and pharmacological neuromodulation studies in spinal cord injury plus neuromechanical modeling that the human lumbar cord can produce rhythmic muscle activation resembling CPG activity of the isolated animal spinal cord in the absence of volitional control and step-specific sensory feedback, and that CPGs may contribute to specific phases of the step cycle while serving as a feedforward component that simplifies supraspinal control of step-cycle frequency for a targeted speed.
animal_study: The proposed phase-specific CPG contribution to normal locomotion could be tested in animals by combining stimulation-elicited spinal rhythms with graded deafferentation during treadmill locomotion, dissociating feedforward CPG output from sensory-driven components.
robot_sim: Add a feedforward CPG component that sets step-cycle frequency for a targeted speed and reduces supraspinal control burden; ablate it and measure the added control complexity or gait degradation in a neuromechanical walker.

notes: Combines patch-clamp recording with holographic glutamate uncaging in mice to reveal focal, layered V3 premotor modules: ventromedial V3 interneurons synapse onto ventrolateral V3 interneurons, which contact ipsilateral motoneurons, while motoneurons return recurrent excitatory glutamatergic input to V3 interneurons, a substrate for well-timed, spatially specific movement.
animal_study: Optogenetically silence the ventrolateral V3-to-motoneuron connection or the motoneuron-to-V3 recurrent excitation during locomotion to test their contributions to the timing precision and spatial specificity of motor output.
robot_sim: Add a two-layer excitatory premotor module (ventromedial to ventrolateral V3 to motoneuron) with motoneuron recurrent excitation back to the premotor layer; ablate the recurrent branch and measure degradation of burst-timing precision.
flags: Motoneuron-to-V3 recurrent glutamatergic excitation is a recurrent-excitation motif absent from the Feedback vocabulary (existing recurrent/Renshaw entries are inhibitory).

notes: Modeling study showing that a locomotor CPG of conditionally bursting flexor and extensor half-center populations with reciprocal inhibition and independent external drives can operate in distinct regimes consistent with competing experimental concepts (quasi-symmetric, flexor-driven, or both half-centers intrinsically rhythmic), with oscillation frequency and phase durations in each regime controlled by the regime-dependent expression of intrinsic rhythmic capability and by escape versus release phase-transition mechanisms, reconciling seemingly contradictory data on CPG organization.
animal_study: Measure phase durations and cycle frequency across locomotor speeds in reduced preparations to seek the regime-dependent signatures the model predicts, distinguishing flexor-driven from half-center operation via stance/swing duration relationships.
robot_sim: Implement conditionally bursting half-centers with reciprocal inhibition and independent drives; sweep drives to demonstrate regime transitions and use escape/release dynamics as the tuning knobs for oscillation frequency and phase durations in an RG core.

notes: Distills cat and human locomotion into design principles for walking robots: control at three levels (actuator/motoneuron, whole-limb flexion-extension oscillators with mutual inhibition, interlimb coordination), with the most essential feedback at the limb level, where activation of the extensor part of the limb oscillator must be triggered by feedback signalling onset of loading via limb load sensors, and flexor activation must require unloading below a threshold plus a hip position within the normal end-of-stance range.
animal_study: Independently manipulate limb loading and hip position during stepping in decerebrate cats to isolate each factor's causal contribution to the flexion-versus-extension decision, as the proposed control rules predict.
robot_sim: Implement the three-level architecture with limb-level decision rules: extensor oscillator activation on limb loading (load-sensor threshold) and flexor initiation gated on unloading below threshold together with hip position in the end-of-stance range; ablate each rule and quantify gait robustness loss.
flags: Load-triggered extensor activation and unload-gated flexor initiation are described functionally without afferent types (Ib-like in the cat literature) and fit no exact vocabulary entry; feedback left empty rather than asserting Ib.

notes: Uses split-belt experiments in intact and spinal cats together with mathematical modeling of CPG circuits to support a state-dependent organization: with increasing excitatory input or locomotor speed, the rhythmogenic mechanism of each limb's rhythm generator changes from flexor-driven rhythmicity toward a classical half-center mechanism, with specific commissural interactions between left and right rhythm generators accounting for stance and swing duration changes under symmetric and asymmetric conditions.
animal_study: Split-belt tests across a speed range in spinal versus intact cats, with phased deafferentation, could bound the sensory contribution to the drive-dependent regime transition attributed to the rhythm generators.
robot_sim: Build a two-level CPG with a separate rhythm generator per limb and commissural interactions; reproduce stance and swing duration changes under symmetric and asymmetric (split-belt) drives and verify that the flexor-driven-to-half-center regime switch emerges with increasing drive.

notes: Introduces N-step capturability, the ability of a legged system to come to a stop without falling within N or fewer steps, as a practical stability criterion, and demonstrates a controller using 1-step capture-region step placement and instantaneous capture point control on a 3D force-controlled biped that recovers from pushes up to 21 Ns while balancing on one leg and 15 Ns while walking, and walks across randomly placed stepping stones.
robot_sim: Implement 1-step capture-region step placement and instantaneous capture point control as a balance supervisor atop a biped; test push-recovery envelopes and stepping-stone walking, and compare against purely reflex-based recovery strategies.
flags: Robotics control paper (capturability framework) with no neural or afferent content; kept as a balance-framework reference. Scope decision for Ben.

notes: Reviews molluscan feeding, postural control in cats and humans, locomotion simulations in lamprey, insect, cat and salamander, and rat vibrissal sensing to argue that adaptive behavior emerges from nervous-system-body-environment interaction: control is shared between nervous system and periphery, neural activity organizes degrees of freedom into biomechanically meaningful subsets, mechanics alone can play crucial roles in enforcing gait patterns, and the mechanics of sensors is crucial for their function.
animal_study: Perturb peripheral mechanics (limb inertia, muscle properties, sensor mechanics) while recording neural compensation across the reviewed preparations, dissociating mechanical from neural contributions to gait enforcement.
robot_sim: Embed morphologically realistic muscle and sensor mechanics so that body dynamics contribute to gait enforcement (preflexes); progressively remove neural correction loops and quantify the locomotor stability retained by mechanics alone.

notes: In 46 stepping neonates, interlimb coordination is variable (including 2:1 locking episodes and activity deletions on a blocked side), hip-position effects are strictly ipsilateral (backward hip position engaging hip flexors, flexed position engaging hip extensors), sudden posterior release of a blocked limb elicits immediate swing initiation, and extensor muscles show load responses at midstance, indicating neonatal networks with independent per-limb pattern generators and load and hip-position feedback but incomplete sensory modulation relative to mature locomotion.
animal_study: Apply matched limb-blocking stepping protocols across immature animals of different species to determine which interlimb coordination features mature after birth and how closely neonatal networks match spinal mammalian preparations.
robot_sim: Model per-limb flexor and extensor pattern generators with hip-position and load feedback but weak interlimb coupling; reproduce 2:1 coordination episodes and activity deletions, then strengthen coupling parameters toward mature alternation.
flags: Neonatal load (midstance extensor activation) and hip-position (release-triggered swing) feedback rules are described without afferent types; candidate vocabulary additions for Ben.

notes: Develops the dorsal spinocerebellar tract system as a model showing that spinal proprioceptive processing produces a global representation of whole-limb parameters rather than a muscle-by-muscle or joint-by-joint code, with the functional organization originating in the biomechanical linkages of the limb and a distributed spinal processing network.
animal_study: Record dorsal spinocerebellar tract neurons during controlled multi-joint limb movements versus isolated joint rotations to test the whole-limb versus joint-by-joint coding framework.
robot_sim: Replace muscle-by-muscle proprioceptive feedback in a locomotor controller with a spinocerebellar-like whole-limb kinematic encoding stage, and test whether the global representation improves interjoint coordination and balance relative to a joint-by-joint representation.
flags: Abstract does not name the species (DSCT work is classically cat); animals left empty per the grounding rule.

notes: Using Vglut2-ChR2 mice, photostimulation of either the lumbar spinal cord or the caudal hindbrain was sufficient to both initiate and maintain locomotor-like activity, directly demonstrating that glutamatergic neurons in the spinal cord are critical for initiating or maintaining the locomotor rhythm and that activation of hindbrain locomotor command regions can directly activate the spinal locomotor network.
animal_study: Silence Vglut2-positive spinal populations during ongoing locomotion, or sweep stimulation frequency and location, to dissociate the rhythmogenic versus command roles of spinal and hindbrain glutamatergic neurons.
robot_sim: Model locomotion initiation as a tonic excitatory glutamatergic drive channel that both starts and sustains the rhythm generator; ablating it should reproduce failure of locomotor initiation while leaving the remaining network structure intact.

notes: Identifies two physiologically and topographically distinct V3 interneuron subpopulations in the mature mouse spinal cord: ventral lamina-VIII cells with simple morphology and rapid tonic firing, active during running in a manner suggesting a premotor role, and dorsal cells with complex morphology, strong spike-frequency adaptation, large sag voltages and post-inhibitory rebound (consistent with HCN and T-type calcium currents), active during swimming in a manner suggesting a sensory-relay role.
animal_study: Separately silence ventral versus dorsal V3 subpopulations during running and swimming to causally test the premotor versus sensory-relay role assignments inferred from their task-dependent activity.
robot_sim: Split the commissural excitatory population in a CPG model into tonic-firing premotor and adapting rebound-capable relay subtypes with HCN- and T-type-like currents; test whether differential recruitment across gaits preserves rhythm robustness.

notes: Identifies V0g ascending neurons as a subtype of the V0 family integrated in lumbar sensorimotor circuits and specifically required for execution of the precise limb movements of skilled locomotion, revealing a previously unappreciated role for ascending spinal neurons in adjusting body movements to the demands of challenging locomotor tasks.
animal_study: Acute silencing of V0g ascending neurons during skilled versus simple locomotor tasks would test the behavioral specificity of the precision deficit, dissociating skill-level adjustments from basic walking.
robot_sim: Implement an ascending precision-correction pathway (V0g analog) that modulates limb-movement precision only in high-demand locomotion modes; ablate it in simulation and quantify loss of foot-placement precision on demanding terrain.

notes: In walking humans, electrical stimulation at the ankle produced phase- and intensity-dependent reflex effects: low-intensity swing-phase stimuli suppressed tibialis anterior activity, high-intensity stimuli facilitated it (largest mid-swing and correlated with exaggerated dorsiflexion), and some subjects showed a phase-dependent reversal from swing-phase tibialis anterior responses to gastrocnemius facilitation during early stance, demonstrating central gating and modulation of reflex transmission rather than simple scaling of ongoing EMG.
animal_study: Replicate the phase-dependent stimulation protocol with identified afferent stimulation in decerebrate walking cats to localize the spinal circuitry underlying the observed gating and reflex reversal.
robot_sim: Implement phase- and intensity-dependent reflex gating in a neuromechanical walker: ankle-afferent stimulation suppresses tibialis anterior in swing at low intensity, facilitates it at high intensity, and reverses to gastrocnemius facilitation in early stance; test the balance contribution during perturbations.
flags: Ankle nerve (tibial/sural) stimulation at perception threshold; the abstract does not specify the afferent class (likely cutaneous/FRA-class), so 'Cutaneous stance modification' was not asserted and feedback was left empty.

notes: Reviews brainstem initiation of locomotion: c-fos-labeled active cells during locomotion localize the mesencephalic locomotor region across the periaqueductal gray, cuneiform nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, and locus coeruleus, with different subsets of locomotor nuclei apparently activated in different behavioral contexts (exploratory, appetitive, defensive), implying that lesion studies must be interpreted relative to the nuclei active in the specific locomotor task tested.
animal_study: Context-specific c-fos mapping combined with stimulation or lesions of individual mesencephalic locomotor region nuclei during exploratory versus defensive locomotion would test the context-dependent recruitment scheme.
robot_sim: Implement a supraspinal initiation module with context-selective drives (exploratory, appetitive, defensive) converging on the spinal locomotor network, mimicking the brainstem command structure; ablate submodules to mirror the lesion-study interpretation caveats.

notes: Reviews insect six-legged walking: how leg central pattern generators interact with sensory signals from the leg in generating single-leg stepping, how those interactions are reconfigured for forward and backward walking, curve walking, and speed changes, and how descending signals from the brain mediate initiation, maintenance, modification, and cessation of walking, with emphasis on knowledge gaps addressable by neurogenetic approaches.
animal_study: Neurogenetic silencing of identified leg sensory organs or CPG interneurons during free walking across directions and speeds in insects, targeting the intersegmental coordination gaps the review identifies.
robot_sim: Implement hexapod leg CPGs coupled to leg sensory signals with reconfigurable interactions for backward walking, curve walking, and speed changes; ablate individual sensory channels to quantify loss of motor flexibility.

notes: Shows that extensor group I afferents' oligosynaptic inhibition of extensor motoneurons at rest is replaced by oligosynaptic excitation not only during fictive locomotion but also during fictive scratching and fictive weight support, with extensor group I input affecting burst amplitude and timing similarly across tasks, evidence for state-dependent opening of excitatory group I reflex pathways during multiple motor behaviors and for a common rhythm-generating network shared by scratching and locomotion.
animal_study: Test the task-generality of the excitatory group I pathway by measuring extensor group I effects during additional motor behaviors, and dissociate the scratching and locomotion rhythms with targeted spinal lesions to test the common-network hypothesis.
robot_sim: Implement state-dependent group I extensor reflex pathways that switch from inhibitory at rest to excitatory during locomotor activity across multiple motor tasks; ablating the state switch should remove extensor load regulation during stance.
flags: Abstract never names the species (fictive locomotion/scratching/weight-support preparation, almost certainly cat); animals left empty per the grounding rule. 'Extensor group I' decomposed as Ia+Ib; the excitation is called oligosynaptic, so it was not mapped to 'Ib disynaptic excitation' or 'Ib excitatory'.
